fields.expected: I'd want to work on research infrastructure, specifically technical systems for evaluating scientific work. Over the past year I've studied independently how research gets funded and selected, reading through the history from patronage to the German research university to Bell Labs to the postwar NIH/NSF project-grant model, and talking with researchers, research administrators, economists, and people building alternative research organizations like FROs. I started out convinced that grant-writing overhead was the main constraint on science. I now think the bigger effect is selection: researchers learn which ideas are legible enough to survive peer review and never attempt the ones that are hard to justify in advance. What interests me now is that AI is making generation cheap, including literature search, analysis, and hypothesis testing, while evaluation stays scarce because reviewer time and domain expertise don't scale. So I'd want to build the judgment layer: methodological validation, provenance, evidence tracing, uncertainty, and explicit escalation to human experts when the system can't decide. I got pulled toward this at Intelehealth, where I built an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes. Generating an answer was easy; deciding whether to trust it was the real problem.

fields.expected: The hardest one was estimating sleep without a wearable for ClarityAtlas, the iOS product I built and lead technically. The constraint was that most of our pilot users at Hopkins didn't own a watch, so anything that assumed continuous wrist accelerometry was useless to us. I had to infer sleep and wake periods from what a phone actually knows: HealthKit and Core Motion signals like step count, gait speed, movement patterns, and phone-interaction gaps. The problem is that absence of signal is ambiguous. A phone sitting still on a desk for three hours looks a lot like a person sleeping, and a user who wakes at 3am and doesn't touch their phone looks like continuous sleep. I ended up building the estimator around combinations of signals rather than any single one, and testing against the sessions where users told us we were wrong. I also built backend services on Supabase for behavioral comparison, including a "Sleep Twins" matching system using standardized features and weighted distance. We shipped it into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users, which is where most of the real failure modes actually showed up.

fields.expected: During Hopkins' Lighting of the Quads, my cofounders and I realized President Ron Daniels was somewhere nearby. We walked over to Garland Hall, saw him through the locked doors, and knocked until someone let us in long enough to pitch ClarityAtlas. It was a slightly ridiculous thing to do and it worked. That conversation turned into a formal meeting months later with him and leadership from the Johns Hopkins Data Science and AI Institute. The outcome is technically on my resume, but the knocking isn't, and the knocking is the part I'm proud of. I spent most of high school and early college assuming the way you get access to people is by accumulating enough credentials that someone eventually invites you. Building ClarityAtlas taught me that shipping the product is maybe half the work. Recruiting the first 30 users, getting institutional buy-in, and repeatedly explaining to skeptical people why the thing should exist mattered as much as the Swift code. Being willing to knock on a locked door is a small version of that, but it's the habit I'd least want to lose.

fields.expected: The Software Engineer role resonates more with what I want to do next, which is why I applied to Infrastructure. The work I've enjoyed most has been owning the layers underneath a product rather than the last mile of a specific deployment. At Summer Atlantic Capital I built and own major parts of the ML and data infrastructure for an anomaly-detection system: the repository and CI scaffold, the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI microservice, and the public detection API, plus the temporal sequence models and the learning-to-rank layer that prioritizes alerts. The part I care about there isn't model accuracy in isolation, it's that an anomaly system producing too many alerts just creates a second problem. I think similarly about correctness boundaries. In a Playwright job-application agent I built, I used SQLite as the single source of truth because browser automation gets dangerous when state diverges across processes, put every mutating capability behind fail-closed flags that never default on, and made free-text and demographic fields architecturally unfillable so they always generate a human-review item. That instinct, designing the substrate so bad states are hard to reach, is what pulls me toward infrastructure over FDE.
